Broth
brŏth
n. (the liquor in which flesh has been boiled)
Old English broth, from the same root as brew. In the Authorized Version it appears at two opposite tables: Gideon's offering under the oak, and the idolaters' vessels of Isaiah 65.

Biblical Definition

Gideon, having been told he should save Israel and asking for a sign, went in and made ready a kid and unleavened cakes, put the flesh in a basket and the broth in a pot, and brought it out to the angel under the oak (Jdg 6:19). The instruction he received turned the meal into a sacrifice: “Take the flesh and the unleavened cakes, and lay them upon this rock, and pour out the broth” (Jdg 6:20). What Gideon had prepared as hospitality was poured out on a rock, and fire rose out of the rock and consumed it. He had meant to feed a guest; he was taught to worship. Isaiah shows the other table: a rebellious people “which remain among the graves, and lodge in the monuments, which eat swine's flesh, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels” (Isa 65:4) — necromancy and forbidden meat together, with the pot as the evidence. The Authorized Version thus uses this small domestic word to mark two possibilities for anything a man prepares: it may be poured out on the rock and consumed by God's own fire, or it may sit in his vessels as an abomination.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines broth as liquor in which flesh has been boiled and its substance extracted; a decoction of flesh, usually with vegetables.

BROTH, n. Liquor in which flesh has been boiled and its substance extracted.

2. A decoction of flesh, usually with rice or other ingredients.

Take the flesh and the unleavened cakes, and lay them upon this rock, and pour out the broth. Judges vi.

Key Scripture

Jdg 6:20 — "And the angel of God said unto him, Take the flesh and the unleavened cakes, and lay them upon this rock, and pour out the broth. And he did so."

Isa 65:4 — "Which remain among the graves, and lodge in the monuments, which eat swine's flesh, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels;"

Jdg 6:21 — "Then the angel of the LORD put forth the end of the staff that was in his hand, and touched the flesh and the unleavened cakes; and there rose up fire out of the rock, and consumed the flesh and the unleavened cakes. Then the angel of the LORD departed out of his sight."

Modern Corruption

Gideon's meal is often preached as a lesson in hospitality or in seeking signs, and the actual turn of the scene — a supper commanded to be poured out as a sacrifice — is passed over.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Broth is broth. But the scene under the oak at Ophrah deserves better handling than it usually gets. Gideon prepared a costly meal — a whole kid and an ephah of flour in a season when Midian had left Israel nothing — and he brought it out as food for a guest. The angel would not eat it. Lay it on this rock, and pour out the broth: that is, this is not a dinner, it is an offering, and the rock is an altar. Fire rose out of the rock and took it, and Gideon, who had begun the conversation arguing that the LORD had forsaken them, built an altar there and called it Jehovahshalom. The principle to recover is that God frequently accepts what we bring by transforming what it is for. A man offers his work, his house, his money, his gift, as hospitality toward God — something done for Him on his own terms — and finds it commanded onto the rock instead, poured out, consumed, and answered with fire. Isaiah 65:4 is the alternative in the same idiom: a pot kept in one's own vessels, full of what God forbade.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew maraq (H4839), broth, the liquor of boiled flesh; paraq, to pour out; bashal (H1310), to boil or seethe.

expand to see more

Hebrew maraq (H4839) — broth, soup, the liquor of boiled flesh; used only of Gideon's pot and of the idolaters' vessels; Judges 6:19-20, Isaiah 65:4.

Hebrew bashal (H1310) — to boil, to seethe; the cooking that produces the broth; Judges 6:19, Exodus 12:9.

Hebrew tsuwr (H6697) — a rock; the rock at Ophrah that became an altar and gave up fire; Judges 6:20-21, Deuteronomy 32:4.

Usage

"“Lay them upon this rock, and pour out the broth” — a supper turned into a sacrifice."

"“There rose up fire out of the rock” — the answer to what was poured out."

"“Broth of abominable things is in their vessels” — the other table, kept in a man's own pot."
